title: Anxiety, Freedom, and Authenticity
text:
Søren Kierkegaard regarded anxiety not as a mere malfunction of the mind but as the dizziness of freedom. When a person confronts the infinite possibilities open to them, they experience a vertigo that reveals how much depends on their own choices. This anxiety, he argued, is not something to be eliminated but understood.

Later thinkers developed this insight in different directions. Martin Heidegger described everyday life as a condition in which people drift into roles dictated by 'the they', escaping the burden of owning their existence. Only through a confrontation with death, he suggested, can one become authentically oneself.

options: A mere malfunction of the mind
A condition that must be eliminated

questions.text: According to Heidegger, what can help a person become authentically themselves?
options: Following the roles set by 'the they'

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about people who drift into roles dictated by 'the they'?
options: They have fully embraced their freedom
They avoid the burden of owning their own existence
They understand death better than others
They experience no anxiety at all

questions.text: What common thread links Kierkegaard and Heidegger?
options: Both treat anxiety as something trivial
Both see authentic existence as demanding a confrontation with one's own freedom
Both reject the importance of individual choice

vocabulary.definition: a persistent feeling of worry or unease about uncertain outcomes
a heavy responsibility or duty that is difficult to bear
in a genuine way that reflects one's true self

paragraph_translations: Серен Кьеркегор рассматривал тревогу не как простой сбой работы разума, а как головокружение свободы. Когда человек сталкивается с бесконечными возможностями, открытыми перед ним, он испытывает головокружение, которое показывает, сколько зависит от его собственного выбора. Эту тревогу, утверждал он, не нужно устранять, её нужно понять.

Более поздние мыслители развили это понимание в разных направлениях. Мартин Хайдеггер описывал повседневную жизнь как состояние, в котором люди незаметно погружаются в роли, навязанные «ими», избегая бремени владения собственным существованием. Лишь через встречу со смертью, полагал он, человек может подлинно стать самим собой.
